doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: English studies, Korean War draft and the family's leftist politics
summary: He took English courses, then was drafted just after graduation but never sent to Korea, which he blames on his family's Communist ties.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I was a freshman you know, I was a freshman, my God. I was 18 years old, What did I know? But yeah for me it was a good background obviously to be well read. And I took it for granted that I was going to study English literature, which I did. I took I think all the courses in English literature that Hamilton offered at that time except Shakespeare which I figured I knew enough about anyway. And Howard Nemerov was my comp teacher, the great poet, well certainly well known poet, now dead. Howard was at Hamilton for several years and was teaching English comp and he wrote a novel when he was up there, I think called Dance Out the Answer which probably is kicking around and was an academic novel and how much of it bore on Hamilton I have no idea but he was there. So I had that literary background. But I never, I didn’t know what I wanted to do. I had graduated from college and I owed some money. I’d never managed to pay my bills. And so I knew that I had to work that off. So I got a job just cutting lawns and whatever, some physical labor to earn some money and pay that off and then get on with it. Well of course the Korean War started within a week after graduation. So within a couple of months I was gone. And fortunately I never got sent to Korea because I would have been dead meat, because that was right at the beginning. I mean it would have been very, very bad. That was a very bad war, very bad. But I was on the list to go three times, and I had shots, I had the whole series of shots for the Far East. And every time, at the last minute they piled the guys in the truck and the Sergeant would be calling out everybody’s name and I’d still be standing there. Three times I was left there. And I can only think that they knew that the government had got me pinpointed because too many of the members of my family were Communists. And my aunt, I have on good testimony, was a card carrying member of the Communist party, but I know for sure she was cited by the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1939. So she was a public figure to some extent. She’d been involved in politics in New York City, she’d been involved with all sorts of, you know, the Milk Committee and that kind of thing, the Consumers Committee and various things of that kind. And my uncle was an editor first on the New Republic and then on the New Masses. So all of this was public. And I can only assume that this was in my dossier somewhere and they weren’t going to send me.
I was thinking, if I do the math right, according to your birthdate, you almost would have been draftable at the end of World War II, right?
I missed it by a year.
By a year, okay. Can you recall back then thinking that that was going to be a possibility if this war doesn’t wind down or end? Was that a concern of yours? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
